rationale: A wins because it refuses the easy lie. Its best line is the adult in the room: "the fact block pairs the two but never connects them, and a reporter will ask." B has useful instincts, but it keeps writing checks the facts cannot cash, especially "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" and "Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices." That is not framing; that is smuggling causality through the headline and hoping the caveat underneath bails you out.
gaps_in_A: "Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory" is plausible beat context, but it is still an unsupported broad claim. It should be softened or tied to outside proof before pitching.
The set misses a possible investor/operator margin angle, but A is right not to elevate it without labor-cost figures. That omission is discipline, not laziness.
"Decay: 24hr" on the price-hold angle may be too harsh because food inflation and menu pricing have a longer trade/business tail, but the urgency logic is defensible.
gaps_in_B: "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" invents a causal link the update does not give. The set later admits the link is "implied but not proven," which means the headline is already guilty.
"Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices" is worse: the company did not say that in the supplied facts. You cannot launder an analyst question into a company claim.
"Its Competitors Are Taking Notes" is unsupported color. No competitor reaction or behavior was supplied, so this is headline theater.

The consumer-pricing angle and the investor-margin angle are partially the same story in different shoes: automation as the mechanism for holding prices/margins. One can survive, but not both without harder financial proof.
